title: Boss: the change machine
summary: Split, swap and convert values without losing a single penny.

steps.title: Module boss
body: Four small functions. Each uses boxes, integer division, remainder or careful number types. Trace your own code on paper before you run it: that is the habit this topic builds.

steps.title: Clock time
prompt: Write `string Clock(int totalMinutes)` that turns minutes since midnight into `H:MM` on a 24-hour clock. Minutes always have two digits.
`Clock(135)` is `"2:15"`, `Clock(605)` is `"10:05"`, `Clock(0)` is `"0:00"`. Input is between 0 and 1439.
hints: `{minutes:D2}` in an interpolated string pads to two digits.

steps.title: Fewest coins
prompt: Write `int[] Coins(int pence)` returning how many 50p, 20p, 10p, 5p, 2p and 1p coins make up `pence` using the fewest coins (always take the biggest coin that fits).
hints: For each coin size: how many fit is `pence / size`, and what is left is `pence % size`.
Keep the sizes in an array and update `pence` after each one.

steps.title: Sort three
prompt: Write `int[] SortThree(int a, int b, int c)` that returns the three values smallest first, using only comparisons and swaps (no `Array.Sort`, no LINQ).
solution: int[] SortThree(int a, int b, int c)
if (a > b) { t = a; a = b; b = t; }
if (b > c) { t = b; b = c; c = t; }
if (a > b) { t = a; a = b; b = t; }
hints: If `a > b`, swap them with a temp box. Then do the same for `b` and `c`.
After those two swaps the largest is in `c`, but `a` and `b` may still be out of order. Compare them once more.

steps.title: Split the bill
prompt: Write `int[] Split(int totalPence, int people)` that shares a bill as evenly as possible in whole pence. Everyone pays the same, except the first few people each pay **one penny more** to cover the remainder. The amounts must add up to the total exactly.
hints: The basic share is `totalPence / people`. The pennies left over are `totalPence % people`.
Person `i` pays one extra penny when `i` is less than the leftover count.

steps.title: Delve's shop
prompt: Delve's merchant counts money the old way: **1 gold = 20 silver**, **1 silver = 12 copper** (so 1 gold is 240 copper). The game keeps your purse as one number of copper; this piece turns it into coins people can read.
- **`static int ToCopper(int gold, int silver, int copper)`**: `ToCopper(1, 2, 3)` is 267.
- **`static string Coins(int copper)`**: as `"Xg Ys Zc"`, always all three. `Coins(267)` is `"1g 2s 3c"`, `Coins(180)` is `"0g 15s 0c"`, `Coins(0)` is `"0g 0s 0c"`.

- **`static string Change(int paid, int price)`**: what is left after paying `price` out of `paid`, written with `Coins`, or `"not enough"` when `paid` is less than `price`. `Change(240, 180)` is `"0g 5s 0c"`.
`Change` must **call** `Coins` rather than repeat its maths.
starter: static int ToCopper(int gold, int silver, int copper)
static string Change(int paid, int price)
solution: static int ToCopper(int gold, int silver, int copper)
static string Change(int paid, int price)
template: Dojo.Eq("Coins(719): 11 copper does not become a silver", "2g 19s 11c", Coins(719));

forbid.message: Every function starts with `static` (Delve keeps its pieces in one static class)

hints: Gold is the number of whole 240s. What is left after the gold, `copper % 240`, holds the silver: how many whole 12s?
The copper coins are what is left after all whole silvers: `copper % 12` works directly, because 240 is a multiple of 12.

build.title: The shop
build.unlocks: Delve's purse shows gold, silver and copper, and the merchant gives correct change.
